Floating-point addition is not associative because real numbers must be represented with a finite number of bits. Modern hardware generally follows IEEE 754 formats, such as binary32 or binary64, which store only a limited number of significant binary digits. Whenever an exact result cannot be represented, the processor rounds it to a nearby representable value. Consequently, the rounded value of (a + b) + c can differ from that of a + (b + c), even though the two expressions are identical in exact arithmetic.

The difference arises most clearly when the operands have very different magnitudes or when cancellation occurs. If a small value is added to a much larger value, the small contribution may fall below the available precision and be rounded away. If the large value is later canceled by another large value, that lost contribution cannot be recovered. With a different grouping, the cancellation might occur first, allowing the small value to remain. Each individual operation usually introduces only a tiny rounding error, but a long sequence of additions can accumulate and propagate such differences.

Large matrix multiplications contain many dot products. Each output element is computed as a sum of products, and that sum may contain thousands or millions of terms. A sequential implementation might add those terms from left to right, while a parallel CPU implementation may divide them among threads and combine partial sums in a tree. A GPU may use a different tree based on thread blocks, warp scheduling, tiling, or specialized matrix hardware. Libraries may also choose different algorithms depending on matrix dimensions, processor type, thread count, or available instructions. Fused multiply-add instructions can produce still another result because they compute a product and addition with one final rounding rather than rounding the product separately.

Since these methods reduce terms in different orders, they can generate slightly different output values even when they use the same inputs and nominal precision. The discrepancies are often only a few units in the last place, but they can become larger for ill-conditioned problems, sums with extensive cancellation, or very long reductions. Subsequent computations may amplify them.

Thus, repeated matrix multiplications are not necessarily bitwise reproducible across hardware, libraries, thread counts, or even runs if scheduling changes dynamically. Numerical results should usually be compared with appropriate tolerances rather than exact equality. When bitwise reproducibility is required, software must enforce a deterministic reduction order or use reproducible summation methods, typically at some cost in speed, memory, or parallel scalability.
